questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 6 & -3 \\ -12 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-6) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $1$st row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107 & 215 & 100\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107+0 & 215+0 & 99+1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107+0 & 215+0 & 99+1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107 & 215 & 99\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107 & 215 & 99\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}107 & 215 \\ 6 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =107\cdot 8-215\cdot 6 \\  & =-434\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 91 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90+1 & 92+0 & 93+0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 90 & 92 & 93 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 90 & 92 & 93\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 92 & 93\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 93-6\cdot 92) \\  & =-(279-552) \\  & =273\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $1$st row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}97 & 98 & 99 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}96+1 & 98+0 & 99+0 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}96+1 & 98+0 & 99+0 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}96 & 98 & 99 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $1$st row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}96 & 98 & 99 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 2 \\ 96 & 98 & 99\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 98 & 99\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot 99-2\cdot 98 \\  & =396-196 \\  & =200\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
questions.problem: Let $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ be square matrices. If $A=B\cdot C,$  $|B|=-15$ and $|{C}^{-1}|=3$, find $|A|.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

Also, given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $M,$ we have

$$
det({M}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(M)}.
$$

Since $|C|=\frac{1}{|{C}^{-1}|}$, we get $|C|=\frac{1}{3}.$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|B|\cdot |C| \\  & =(-15)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$
